title: Raconter autrement
intro: Imaginer l'impossible avec if et I wish, raconter à la voix passive, relier tes idées avec who, which et whose, et maîtriser tes premiers phrasal verbs.

boss.name: Madame Passive
boss.taunt: Ici, ce n'est pas toi qui agis : c'est toi qui seras battu ! Si tu étais plus fort, tu gagnerais… mais tu ne l'es pas.
boss.defeat: J'ai été… battue ? Par toi ?! C'est écrit à la voix passive, mais ça fait mal quand même.

units.title: Et si… ?
units.goal: Imaginer des situations irréelles et donner des conseils avec if + passé, would et I wish.

lesson.text: Le **deuxième conditionnel** sert à imaginer : une situation **irréelle** ou **peu probable**, maintenant ou dans le futur. En français : « Si j'avais…, je ferais… ».

lesson.title: La formule
lesson.text: [[If]] + passé, [[would]] + verbe de base. [[If I had a million dollars, I would buy an island.]] Ici, le passé ne parle **pas** du passé : il montre que c'est imaginaire. [[would]] devient souvent [[I'd]], [[you'd]], [[we'd]]. On peut aussi utiliser [[could]] (pourrais) : [[If I had wings, I could fly.]]

lesson.title: Was ou were ?
lesson.text: Après [[if]] et [[wish]], l'anglais soigné utilise **were** avec tous les sujets : [[If I were rich…]], [[If she were here…]]. À l'oral, beaucoup de gens disent [[was]] ([[If I was rich]]), et c'est accepté : dans ce jeu, quand les deux sont possibles, les deux sont acceptés. **Mais dans l'expression figée [[If I were you]] (= à ta place), on dit were.** C'est la forme à connaître pour donner un conseil.

lesson.title: I wish + passé
lesson.text: [[I wish]] + passé = j'aimerais que ce soit différent **maintenant**. [[I wish I had a dog.]] (je n'en ai pas). [[I wish I were taller.]] (je ne suis pas grand). [[I wish I could swim.]] (je ne sais pas nager). Avec une autre personne : [[My brother wishes he lived in Montreal.]]

Piège : en français, « Si j'**aurais** » est une faute… et en anglais aussi ! Jamais [[would]] dans la partie [[if]] : [[If I had]], pas *If I would have*. Et après [[I wish]], jamais de présent : [[I wish I knew]], pas *I wish I know*.

reading.title: The Magic Wand
reading.text:
Last Friday, our teacher, Madame Roy, asked the class a strange question: "What would you do if you had a magic wand for one day?" Everyone had to write a short paragraph.

Samuel wrote that he would make school start at noon. "If classes started later, students would be less tired and would learn more," he explained. Priya wished she could talk to animals. If she understood her cat, she would finally know why it sits on her homework every night.

Ethan's answer surprised everyone. He wrote, "If I had a magic wand, I wouldn't use it for myself. I would give every family in the world clean water and enough food." The class was quiet for a moment.

Then Madame Roy asked a second question: "And if you didn't have a magic wand, what could you do?" Ethan thought about it. "If we organized a bake sale, we could donate the money to a food bank."

The class loved the idea. Next month, they are going to sell cookies and muffins at lunch. Priya says that if her cat helped in the kitchen, the cookies would be terrible!

units.title: La voix passive
units.goal: Dire ce qui est fait, a été fait ou sera fait, avec la voix passive et by.

lesson.text: Phrase active : [[James Naismith invented basketball.]] Phrase passive : [[Basketball was invented by James Naismith.]] Au passif, ce qui **subit** l'action devient le sujet. Celui qui fait l'action arrive après [[by]] (par).

lesson.title: La formule
lesson.text: **be** (au bon temps) + **participe passé**. C'est **be** qui change de temps ; le participe, lui, ne bouge pas. On ajoute [[by]] + la personne seulement si c'est utile.

lesson.title: Quand l'utiliser ?
lesson.text: Quand l'action est plus importante que celui qui la fait, ou quand on ne sait pas qui l'a faite : [[My phone was stolen.]] C'est très fréquent dans les nouvelles, en science et dans les modes d'emploi. Et le « **on** » français se traduit souvent par un passif : « On parle français ici » = [[French is spoken here.]]

Pièges : 1) Ne pas oublier **be** : [[The window was broken]], pas *The window broken*. 2) Connaître les participes irréguliers : [[written]], [[built]], [[made]], [[taken]], [[stolen]], [[sold]], [[eaten]], [[shown]], [[caught]]. 3) « Traduit **en** anglais » = [[translated into English]].

reading.title: The Smart Garbage Can
reading.text:
Every spring, a science fair is organized at Mei's school. This year, more than forty projects were presented, and the winners were chosen by a group of real engineers.

Mei's project was a smart garbage can. It was designed by Mei and her friend Jaden, and it was built with old toys and a small motor. When something is thrown inside, it is sorted automatically: plastic goes to one side and paper goes to the other.

On the day of the fair, the gym was filled with visitors. Mei's garbage can was tested many times. Once, a banana peel was put in the plastic section by mistake, and everyone laughed. Jaden fixed the problem in a few minutes.

At the end of the day, the results were announced. The first prize was won by a boy who built a robot that could water plants. Mei and Jaden came second.

A week later, their invention was mentioned in the local newspaper, and a short video of it has been watched hundreds of times online. Now the smart garbage can is being used in the school cafeteria. Mei hopes that one day, it will be copied by other schools.

units.title: Qui, que, dont
units.goal: Relier deux idées avec who, which, that, whose, where et when, et parler des métiers.

lesson.text: Les **pronoms relatifs** relient deux phrases en une seule : [[I have a friend. She speaks Spanish.]] → [[I have a friend who speaks Spanish.]]

head: Pronom
Pour…
Exemple
rows: une personne ou une chose (sans virgules)
[[the girl whose dad is a pilot]]

lesson.title: Peut-on enlever le pronom ?
lesson.text: Si le pronom est **complément** (il y a un autre sujet juste après), on peut l'enlever : [[the book (that) I read]], [[the boy (who) I saw]]. Mais s'il est **sujet** du verbe qui suit, on le garde : [[the man who lives next door]] (jamais *the man lives next door is…*).

lesson.title: Avec ou sans virgules
lesson.text: Sans virgules = l'information est **essentielle** pour savoir de qui on parle : [[The cousin who lives in Toronto is a nurse.]] (j'ai plusieurs cousins). Avec virgules = information **en plus** : [[My dad, who is a mechanic, can fix anything.]] Avec des virgules : **jamais [[that]]**, et on ne peut pas enlever le pronom.

Pièges de francophone : 1) « le jour **où** » = [[the day when]], pas *the day where* : [[where]] = un lieu seulement. 2) [[whose]] = possession ([[the boy whose sister…]] = le garçon dont la sœur…). Ne le confonds pas avec [[who's]] (= who is). 3) Pas de pronom en double : [[the book that I read]], jamais *the book that I read it*.

grammar.q: I'll never forget the summer ___ we went to Vancouver.
grammar.explain: Un moment (l'été où) : when, pas where.

grammar.q: Dans quelle phrase peut-on enlever le pronom relatif ?
choices: The man who lives next door is a lawyer.
My sister, who is a nurse, works at night.
The cake that my dad made was delicious.
grammar.explain: That est complément (my dad est le sujet de made) : The cake my dad made… Dans les autres, impossible.

grammar.q: Quelle phrase est correcte ?
choices: The phone that I bought it is broken.
The phone what I bought is broken.
The phone who I bought is broken.
The phone I bought is broken.
grammar.explain: Pas de it en double, pas de what, pas de who pour une chose. On peut enlever that.

grammar.q: An electrician is someone ___ repairs electrical problems.
grammar.explain: Personne + sujet du verbe : who (ou that).

grammar.q: Do you know the girl ___ backpack is on the floor?
grammar.explain: Possession : whose.

grammar.q: This is the park ___ we play soccer every weekend.
grammar.explain: Un lieu : where.

grammar.q: My computer, ___ is ten years old, is really slow.
grammar.explain: Une chose avec des virgules : which (jamais that).

grammar.q: Friday is the day ___ we have gym class.
grammar.explain: Un moment : when (ou that). Pas where !

grammar.q: The mechanic which fixed our car was very fast.
grammar.explain: Pour une personne : who ou that, pas which.

grammar.q: The firefighter who's truck is red waved at us.
grammar.explain: Possession : whose. Who's = who is.

grammar.q: This is the hospital which I was born.
grammar.explain: Un lieu (où je suis né) : where.

grammar.q: My sister, that is a lawyer, lives in Toronto.
grammar.explain: Avec des virgules, jamais that : who.

grammar.q: I remember the day where we moved to Ottawa.
grammar.explain: Le jour où = the day when (un moment, pas un lieu).

reading.title: Career Day
reading.text:
Every year, Karim's school organizes a career day. Parents who have interesting jobs come to the school and talk about their work.

The first visitor was Ana's mother, who is a veterinarian. She works in a clinic where people bring their cats, their dogs and even their snakes. She told the students about a parrot that could say hello in three languages.

Next came a firefighter whose son is in grade seven. He showed the students the heavy uniform that firefighters wear, and he let Karim try on the helmet. "The day when I saved a family's cat from a tree was the best day of my career," he said with a smile.

The last visitor was an engineer who designs bridges. Karim expected her talk to be boring, but it was the most interesting one. She explained that the bridges which cross the Ottawa River must be checked regularly, because ice and snow can damage them.

That evening, Karim told his parents about the people he met. "I'm not sure which job I want," he said, "but I know I want a job where I can solve problems."

questions.q: What does Ana's mother do?
What was special about the parrot?
choices: It was saved by a firefighter.
It could say hello in three languages.

questions.q: Who let Karim try on a helmet?
What did Karim think of the engineer's talk?
choices: It was as boring as he expected.
It was much better than he expected.

questions.q: Why must the bridges be checked regularly?
choices: Because ice and snow can damage them
Because the river is too deep

units.title: Phrasal verbs (1)
units.goal: Comprendre et utiliser les phrasal verbs les plus courants, en plaçant bien le pronom.

lesson.text: Un **phrasal verb**, c'est un verbe + un petit mot ([[up]], [[off]], [[on]], [[out]], [[down]], [[after]]…). Le sens change complètement : [[give]] = donner, mais [[give up]] = abandonner !

head: Phrasal verb
Sens
Exemple
rows: manquer de, ne plus avoir de

lesson.title: Séparable : le pronom au milieu !
lesson.text: Beaucoup de phrasal verbs sont **séparables** : le complément peut aller au milieu **ou** à la fin : [[Turn off the radio.]] = [[Turn the radio off.]] Mais avec un **pronom** ([[it]], [[them]], [[her]], [[me]]…), le pronom va **obligatoirement au milieu** : [[Turn it off.]] — jamais *Turn off it*. Séparables : [[turn on]], [[turn off]], [[turn down]], [[put on]], [[take off]], [[pick up]], [[fill out]], [[give up]].

lesson.title: Inséparables : le pronom après
lesson.text: D'autres ne se séparent **jamais** : [[look for]], [[look after]], [[run out of]]. Le complément va toujours à la fin : [[I'm looking for them.]], [[She looks after him.]] Et certains n'ont pas de complément du tout : [[get up]], [[grow up]], [[come back]], [[break down]], [[set off]], [[carry on]].

Piège n° 1 : *Turn off it* ❌ → [[Turn it off]] ✅. Piège n° 2 : traduire mot à mot. [[Look after]] ne veut pas dire « regarder après », mais « s'occuper de ». Et [[take off]] veut dire « enlever » (un manteau) **ou** « décoller » (un avion).

lesson.text: Le sais-tu ? Un même phrasal verb peut avoir plusieurs sens : [[pick up]] veut dire « ramasser », « aller chercher quelqu'un » ou même « apprendre sans effort » : [[I picked up some Spanish on vacation.]]

grammar.q: The music is too loud. Can you ___?
grammar.explain: Avec un pronom, il va au milieu : turn it down. Turn it up = monter le volume.

grammar.q: I can't find my keys. Can you help me ___?
grammar.explain: Chercher = look for (inséparable) : look for them.

grammar.q: « Il s'occupe de son petit frère. » → He ___ his little brother.
grammar.explain: S'occuper de = look after.

grammar.q: It's minus twenty outside. ___ your coat!
grammar.explain: Mettre un vêtement = put on.

grammar.q: We've ___ milk. Can you buy some?
grammar.explain: Manquer de = run out of. Après we've, le participe est run (pas ran).

grammar.q: « Mon père a refusé l'offre. » → My dad ___ the offer.
grammar.explain: Refuser une offre = turn down.

grammar.q: Quelle phrase est correcte ?
choices: She looked them after all day.
She looked after all day them.
She looked after them all day.
grammar.explain: Look after est inséparable : le pronom va après, look after them.

grammar.q: Your shirt is on the floor. Please ___.
grammar.explain: Séparable + pronom : pick it up (le pronom au milieu).

grammar.q: The plane will ___ in ten minutes.
grammar.explain: Pour un avion, décoller = take off.

grammar.q: I was so tired that I almost ___ at the end of the race.
grammar.explain: Give up → gave up au passé.

grammar.q: My parents ___ in Haiti, but now they live in Ottawa.
grammar.explain: Grow up → grew up au passé.

grammar.q: We have to ___ this form before Friday.
grammar.explain: Remplir un formulaire = fill out (ou fill in).

grammar.q: These shoes are too small. ___ and try the blue ones.
grammar.explain: Séparable + pronom : take them off.

grammar.q: I'm looking after my glasses. Have you seen them?
grammar.explain: Chercher = look for. Look after = s'occuper de.

grammar.q: Our car broke up on the highway.
grammar.explain: Tomber en panne = break down.

grammar.q: Put off your hat. It's cold outside!
grammar.explain: Mettre un vêtement = put on.

grammar.q: We run out of bread yesterday.
grammar.explain: Yesterday → passé : ran out of.

grammar.q: My little brother wants to grow down and be a pilot.
grammar.explain: Grandir = grow up.

reading.title: A Camping Trip to Remember
reading.text:
Last July, Emma's family set off on a camping trip to Algonquin Park. They got up at five o'clock, packed the car and left the city before sunrise.

Two hours later, the car broke down on the highway. Emma's dad looked under the car, but he couldn't find out what was wrong. Finally, a tow truck came and picked them up.

The mechanic fixed the car quickly, so the family carried on to the park. But when they arrived, it was raining. They put on their raincoats and tried to build the tent. The wind was so strong that Emma's little brother, Noah, wanted to give up and go home. "Don't give up," said Emma. "Let's look for a better place." They found a spot under some tall trees and finished the tent.

That night, they ran out of dry wood, so they couldn't make a fire. They ate cold sandwiches and turned off their flashlights early.

The next morning, the sun came out. The lake was calm, and a moose was drinking water near their tent. Emma took a photo and smiled. "We have to come back next year," she said.

questions.q: What happened on the highway?
Why did Noah want to go home?
Why couldn't the family make a fire?
choices: They ran out of dry wood.
Fires were not allowed in the park.

questions.q: What did they see the next morning?
choices: A moose drinking near their tent

questions.q: How does Emma feel about the trip at the end?
choices: She regrets it and never wants to camp again.
She is happy and wants to do it again.
She is angry at her dad.
She is scared of the moose.
